text:
Zurich wins the ice hockey tournament at the Centenary

Saturday and Sunday, Monruz's rink was surrounded once again by a large audience who, despite very cold weather, followed the ice hockey tournament at the Centenary with great interest. This sporting event was fully successful; however, we sometimes express a slight regret: why did the three matches start with ten to fifteen minutes of delay?

Zurich beats Montchoisi 12-8 (3-0, 6-3, 3-5)

The Lausanne players began by practicing a game that was somewhat disorganized: defense was very slow and forwards too individual. There was also a clear difference in class between the two teams present, with Zurich playing with much more decisiveness, securing an early three-goal advantage for Urson, Bieler, and Ernst.

During the second third, the Zurichis loosened up slightly, while Montchoisi gradually organized himself and attacked fiercely. This third was thus fairly balanced, without however allowing Zurich to lose control of play. They scored five goals by Bieler (2), Urson, Sylvio Rossi, Boiler, and Gugenbuhl, while Banninger had to allow three shots from the Vaudois, two from Minder, and one from Caseel.

In contrast, in the final third, Montchoisi resolutely attacked again, showing unexpected qualities. The Lausannois Hennsler is particularly energetic and scored three goals. Other well-executed attacks will further reduce the score gap between Beltrami and Caseel. However, the defense fails to contain the Zurichian counterattacks, and well-placed shots by Rossi, Ernst, and Boiler will solidify the victory for the players of the Limmat.

Zurich beats Young Sprinters 10-2 (5-0, 1-2, 4-0)

This match, let's be frank, caused us some disappointment. We hoped for a more balanced struggle; Young Sprinters is certainly capable of better resisting Zurich than it did yesterday morning.

Our players, in truth, can invoke an attenuating circumstance. Hugo Delnon was sick and, as a result, the first Lausanne line was disorganized. Moreover, Reto appeared on the ice only at the beginning of the second third.

The first part of the game saw Zurich enjoy very easy dominance. Bieler, Schubiger, and Lohrer spread panic in our camp and scored five goals one after another.

The second third gave us hope for a situation reversal. Reto is there and seems determined to make it happen. He scores two excellent goals without the goalkeeper Banninger allowing any defensive movement. But the Lausanne team continues to play with some inconsistency. The two Delnon brothers are outplayed by the talented Ulrich, but this line lacks cohesion and will not succeed. Sylvio Rossi, on the other hand, will score a new goal.

The final third was quite monotonous; Zurich is superior and will manage without too much effort to increase its lead with three successful goals scored by Boiler, Gugenbuhl, and Urson.

In the Lausanne camp, let's note the good part of goalkeeper Perrottet and the speed, decisiveness, and ball control of Ulrich.

At Zurich, it is above all worth praising the solidity and a bit of toughness of their defense; the first line formed by Bieler, Lohrer, and Schubiger was far the best line of the tournament.

Young Sprinters beats Montchoisi 5-3 (2-0, 1-2, 2-1)

This match makes us forget the disappointing game played yesterday morning. The two main rivals from France are engaged in a very open and varied struggle.

Note some epic duels between Hans Cattini, Stucki, the two Delnon brothers, and Ulrich. Admitting its shortcomings, our team played honorably and continued to enjoy a slight superiority over its opponent. Reto and Othmar Delnon opened the score in the first third. The Lausanne players concentrated their main effort on the second third, but our line formed by Tinembart and Dr. Grether, as well as goalkeeper Perrottet, performed exceptionally well on Sunday, managing to stop their attacks except for two who allowed Jansky and Beltrami to place the puck at the bottom of the Neuchâtel net.

The final third, where the game becomes quite intense, saw Young Sprinters secure a deserved victory. Jansky first took advantage judiciously of an error in our defense, but Othmar Delnon will once again deceive goalkeeper Ayer twice.

Let's note the excellent work of Ulrich. Fast, pushing to the end every descent without ever losing a pass, he led with skill the attacks of our second line and some of his shots would have earned them the goal.

The tournament results

Following these matches, Zurich wins the tournament by four points, followed by Young Sprinters (2 p.) and Montchoisi, chosen (0 p.).

Zurich wins the first prize of the Centenary and the challenge of the tournament.

Young Sprinters secures the second distinction at the Centenary and the challenge Vuillomenet, rewarding the team for playing with the most fair play. As for Montchoisi, he receives the cup offered by Palace Cinema. B. Ad.

A tour of Young Sprinters in Czechoslovakia

Our ice hockey team was invited to participate in a certain number of matches in Czechoslovakia, including against Prague and Brno. It will depart for this country at the beginning of March and will be strengthened by a few other players from the A1 league.

THE NEWSPAPER
DEPARTMENT OF FISHING
Special Service of the "Ave Garde of Neuchâtel"
Towards a New Kellogg Note
PARIS, 29 (Havas). — A dispatch from New York to the Petit Parisien states that Mr. Kellogg proposes to address the powers with a new note that will incorporate, in a slightly modified form, the first Kellogg formula and may perhaps include an allusion to the safeguarding of existing international guarantees.

In matters concerning the breach of the pact by violating a signatory, it is probable that the note will be accompanied by an annex specifying that the signatories will recover their freedom of action toward any partner who comes to be involved in a war.

As for various other reservations, opinion appears to prevail in the State Department that they will simply be passed over without comment, since governments seem to now agree that they are implicitly contained within the text proposed by Mr. Kellogg.

An Interview with Mr. Venizelos
LONDON, 29 (Havas). — The "Daily Mail" publishes an exposé of the political situation in Greece that was done to its correspondent by Mr. Venizelos. The statesman stated that the cabinet will remain in office until the creation of the Senate and the Council of State as provided by the new constitution.

Despite his desire not to reappear in political life, Mr. Venizelos has been constrained by the insistence of his friends and by the necessity of defending the republic against the royalists, whose press announced as soon as possible the return of George II, son of Constantine. Mr. Venizelos believes that his return will calm the fervor of the royalists who do not want elections with him at the head of the liberal party.

A new incident in Belgrade
-BELGRADE, 29 (Havas). — The correspondent of Belgrade's newspaper announces that the Belgrade police seized two wagons shipped from Italy to Bulgaria at the station under the cover of a commercial caravan bound for Bulgaria, in disguise as a shipment of oranges.

The letter of dispatch states that the wagons carrying munitions and bombs were supposed to contain oranges. The newspaper adds that official circles give no confirmation of this new development, and on the other hand the police refuse to provide information.

A match worth attending
The rental of seats gives rise to riots
PARIS, 29 (Havas). — According to the "Petit Parisien," the rental of seats for the Uruguay-Paraguay match, which will take place on Wednesday, gave rise to serious incidents. 7,500 seats remained to be rented and 30,000 people wanted to attend the match. Serious riots occurred. The police intervened and were forced to charge a saber into the air in full view of the public. About fifty injured were transported to the hospital.

After torrential rains
Disaster in Silesia
BERLIN, 29 (Wolff). — The "Vossische Zeitung" announces that due to continuous rain in Silesia, the territory between Reichenbach and Schweitnitz, about 15 km long and several meters wide, is flooded. The surrounding villages are partially isolated. The fields are filled with mud and the first harvest of hay is destroyed. The plows have been pulled away by the water and several roads are damaged. In the lower part of Reichenbach and Schweitnitz, a number of buildings were blown up. In the upper part of the Weistritz, a complete house was destroyed. In the Riesengebirge, several villages in Czech territory were heavily damaged.

Tunnel crossings
A train collides with a car
Four dead
STOCKHOLM, 29 (Wolff). — A serious accident occurred on Monday at a level crossing near the city of Sala. A car entered a collision with a train traveling at full speed and was derailed by it over a distance of 200 meters and completely destroyed. Two people died on site. Two others died during their transport to the hospital. One fifth is in danger of death and two others are lightly injured.

Another false trail
The murder of Mrs. Wilson
PARIS, 29 (Havas). — A dispatch from the press states that the investigator searching for Mrs. Wilson was arrested yesterday at Truay. Everything suggests that he will not be prosecuted regarding this murder, as he provided an alibi that has been found "exact." It will, however, be maintained in prison, because he was sentenced a few months ago to 90 days' imprisonment for the aforementioned Italian-Serbian incidents.

Manifestations suppressed
BELGRADE, 29 (Avala). — Students attempted to demonstrate in the evening on Belgrade's streets against Italy, but the police, in accordance with formal orders received from the interior ministry, intervened energetically and dispersed the demonstrators.

Peace reigns in Belgrade and other cities.
Buenos Aires, 28 (Havas). — A large bomb exploded yesterday in the residence of Mr. César Aseltra, former Italian lieutenant-colonel, "Oh, I think this attack is the work of anti-fascists." No victims were reported. The house threatens to collapse.

Wilkins and Eielson in Copenhagen
-COPENHAGUE, 29 (Havas). — The aviator Wilkins and Eielson arrived on Monday afternoon by air mail from Oslo. They were escorted by three Danish military aircraft.

The Japanese investigation in Canton
PARIS, 29 (Havas). — The "Petit Journal" publishes the following dispatch from London:

A message from Tokyo announces the return of a government official appointed to investigate the anti-Japanese riots in Canton. The outcome of this investigation will form the basis for a note that the Japanese revolution proposes to send to Great Britain.

The legs of the ostrich
"Annales coloniales" provide an amusing example of Arab thievery:

Mohamed carries two roasted ostriches to the pacha.
Hungry, he rips off a leg from each ostrich and devours it.
Fury of the pacha who, the next day, after eating the ostrich, calls Mohammed:
— You dared offer me ostriches with only one leg?
— Lord, all ostriches have only one leg. See rather here, in the palace courtyard, a dead ostrich. The birds are on one leg. The pacha strikes them in their single legs. The ostriches awaken and escape on two legs.
— Well, I am the pacha.
— Well! responds Mohammed before eating his two ostriches, doubtless you have certainly struck your hands in mine.

ASSEMBLED PARLIAMENT

At the national council, Mr. President delivers a speech to congratulate Mr. Deucher on his 25th anniversary of joining the Federal Council. The assembly rises in honor of Mr. Deucher.

The council adopts a motion by Mr. MOTTÀ requesting the establishment of an appeal mechanism against decisions made by the executive power that could involve a violation of constitutional guarantees.

Disputes regarding the law on arts and crafts are settled, and bills on horse census and agricultural chemical plant construction are voted on. Then the session is adjourned at 10:20 AM.

At the Council of States, Mr. <DE REDING> (Schwytz) reports on the motion by Oyex-Ponnaz concerning subsidizing trade unions for wine sales, adopted in its general text by the national council. Membership is voted on.

Mr. SCHULTHESS (Switzerland) develops his motion advocating an increase in federal subsidies for primary education.

The Council of States has considered Mr. Schulthess' motion.

The president recalls Mr. Deucher's 25th anniversary of joining the Federal Council. The assembly rises in honor of him.

The session is adjourned at 11:25 AM.

text:
If you believe Mme Clark Gable, Pat O'Brien and Warren Williams, famous actors of Hollywood are not jealous.
Would you like to know that thousands of women write passionate love letters to your husband, full of compliant descriptions of their charms? Would you like other women, more daring than the previous ones, to call him night after night and suddenly attach themselves when it is "you" who replies? Or well, when you go out with him, would you support them beating him up with admiring looks or turning towards you with a frown indicating: "Does he find her?" In fact, do you believe that you would not be jealous if you were the wife of a famous movie actor? You doubt it, don't you?
Mrs. Gable is strong—
"Strong"—Mme Clark Gable, to whom unknown people write such letters saying "What a marvelous surprise it is to be the wife of Clark Gable!" is considered one of the most charming women in Hollywood. To hear this, the devil of jealousy hardly troubles her.
—I am flattered that other women find my husband to their liking. It is when they stop being interested in him that I begin to worry, because I realize that his success is due, largely, to his physical attraction to women.
To be jealous is to be weak. In most cases, jealousy is made up of 90% wounded vanity. "Why should people think of me?" asks the wife caught in this state. Well. my personal feeling is that the only thing that truly matters in the world is the harmony existing between a husband and his wife. People's opinions matter little. If Clark meets someone who pleases him more than me, free he will be to him. I will do nothing to hinder his decision, because I believe that love cannot be restrained by chains.
Mrs. Williams is sure of herself...
Perhaps less open-minded, Mrs. Warren Williams' opinion is nevertheless liberal.
— It is not doubtful, she declares, that an actor, especially if he is a handsome boy, encounters in a week or a month more temptations than an ordinary man knows in a lifetime. The wisdom lies in studying his husband before marrying him. Well, I knew Warren for years before becoming his wife. He naturally had the opportunity to meet charming women. Since he asked me to be his, that is what I think, because I preferred him to anyone else. That is on this principle that I have built my life since I married him. Any woman should do the same, because a man always marries the one who most resembles his ideal. She will therefore keep her love as long as she maintains this resemblance. I strive to achieve it and I have all the reasons to believe that I have succeeded. Warren and me are happy because mutual trust is at the foundation of our marriage.
and Mme O'Brien confident...
Even Mrs. Pat O'Brien's manner of speaking.
— One cannot be jealous of the whole world, she says. Well. Pat loves everything. She calls all women "My little boy" or "My dear." but it doesn't matter. Pat is a joker doubled with an Irish accent. My husband is not one of those actors who lower his wife to the backstage plan. He trains me everywhere, on the contrary, and if he happens to be afflicted by autograph seekers, he tells them: "Ask for my wife instead. She is the most important member of the family."
Finally, often when returning from receptions where these more beautiful stars of Hollywood were present, Pat slips into me: "You know, my little boy, I have looked at them well. There isn't one who can match her charms."
René Brest.

Bioiiey won the Tour of Geneva

Two important events for our elite enthusiasts

At the level of amateur elites, the weekend was significant in Geneva. Oscar Plattner, a major representative of this category of potential future champions, had delegated his powers to Gilbert Perrenoud, so that he could closely monitor what was happening on the roads. The National Committee has indeed set its very deliberate intention to establish the best possible team for the Tour de l'Avenir, the Olympics, and the world championships. A full selection program has thus been put in place.

On Sunday afternoon, Gilbert Perrenoud declared himself delighted by what he had seen. Not immediately can it be said that the Swiss runners are in form, but there were no shortage of points of satisfaction: "We see that we are in an important year, a year where travel and honors will be numerous. There is Uruguay, Mexico, medals to sell. That's why our best runners have prepared well, and so too many young people knock on the door...

In fact, these two Geneva races allowed for many lessons. Both races were raced quickly and ran at an excellent quality.

D'OSCHGER...

On Saturday afternoon, on a circuit of sixteen kilometers to be completed eight times, about sixty-five runners took off. Under the sun, which was going to disappear soon and make way for a violent storm, the escape, the good one, came very quickly. Already in the second lap, after a "false start" had occurred—that is, an error of course annulling the efforts of the first daring souls—race was stopped at 9 km 400 from its first departure and then restarted.

It was then that one of the Belgians invited, coldly, tried to leave. He succeeded in company with Rub, Oeschger, Schnetzler, the Swiss champion von Arx, Fischer, and the Romans, Behier (Moudon), Regamey (Yverdon) and Vaucher (Lausanne).

On narrow, winding roads, this escape gained some advantage. First on the peloton, in a group of counter-attacks coming up next, which was going to join. Moreover, there were no more than these men running... The others thought about the lake race for tomorrow and retreated there again, followed by a few more audacious souls: Schnetzler, Spannagel, Birrer and Weber. But their solo attempts were reduced to nothing. And at the end, the peloton split into two.

.
BIOLLEY

This Tour of the Lake — the queen of cycling races, which was last year's 76th edition — had a rather rare course. Daniel Biolley from Fribourg explained it once passed, as winner, the finish line: "It is my sixth race on the lake. And up to now I have noticed that no escape from far away ever succeeds. So I have not led since Versoix (10 km) where we set off. But like at Evian, when we approached the Vinzier pass, we had more than five minutes ahead of our pursuers, and more than ten on the peloton, so I launched myself into the fight."

The race started very early: Brunner—who would quickly disappear—Lier, Hofer and Grin went towards the entrance of the Geneva-Lausanne highway. Rapidly, Biolley, Angelucci, Elliker, Kalt, Rennhard, Rutchmann, Thalmann, Reusser, Adam, Schneider and Melliflio joined him. And, over the course of kilometers, due to some or other mechanical troubles, it remained ten men together at Evian, four of whom left quickly from the first difficult section of the day, four who stayed together until the arrival where a small drama occurred: Lier sprinted, gained but did not realize he had a turn and the distance to cover...

Biolley passed, just like Rennhardt. The two co-riders (from Allegro) had patibulary mines at the finish. Lier cried and Biolley was no happier about it: "Victory belonged to him; he had done a great job of work. But I couldn't get up, because Rennhard had passed."

text:
Reforms and Proletarianization in Austria

I asked a concierge about his relations with the Russian occupants in Vienna. "In the early years," he replied when I saw a Russian approaching, "I alarmed the house, made the women go downstairs, and hid valuable items in a safe place, then I called the police." — And now? — Today, when a Russian comes to us, he says: "Do you need sugar, coffee, tea?" — Do you buy what they offer him?

— Think about it, it's too expensive for us,
we don't have any money.

Too expensive, no money, that's the words used everywhere in Austria today. Indeed, everything is too expensive
for the vast majority of the population.
Too expensive, this large dinner at 20 sh., this fine quality meal at 730 sh., this excellent bottle sold for 20 sh., too expensive even for this small bouquet of flowers, which one would want to offer their charming companion, and for which we are asked 3 sh. Too expensive these Austrian cigarettes, whose best market costs 30 gr. each, while they can be found imported for 1.2 or 15 gr. at the black market. The State, which holds the monopoly on tobacco production, swears its great gods that lowering prices would ruin the business. Of course, since it collects a billion and a half — nine zeros — from tobacco sales. Operating a discount on this illicit gain would be an unprofitable affair. If the customer addresses competition that lurks everywhere, the State will not die of it. It has other taxes to collect.

Everyone is starving: frugal, and we are looking for the responsible party. These 200 million resulting from the sale of American products and which, according to the donor's wish, must be reserved for special jobs; occupation fees that occupants cannot avoid, except for the Americans: the monetary reform carried out in December last year in order to cut short the inflationist movement—that is, to eliminate the enormous surplus of banknotes circulating—which was lacking equivalents in goods;
all these factors, they accuse each other of causing the lack of cash. If they are all three, it is undeniable that after the monetary reform, Austrians lacked money; yet wages and production costs remained the same. At the same time,
goods began to flow onto the market. Some of them had even decreased, such as electric lamps, some textiles, iron, etc. — But how many bars of iron do you buy per day?

Finally, provisions also appeared, but they cost just as much, if not more, than before the reform. The reaction of residents was natural: they bought what was necessary first and foremost—food—and renounced anything that was unnecessary.

One could believe that at least producers and grocery store owners rejoice and bless the current state of affairs. Far from it; they groan like all their compatriots, because Austrian production cannot cover food demand and above all
because Austrians receive only 1,700 calories per year, which allows no one to show any annoyance to these benefactors who offer you everything you need.

They are willing to use their services even more so that the black market prices and those of the gray market have been reduced—not because they have enough to eat, but because they do not have money. Increasingly, the illegal market is transforming into a legal institution, and the private referendum organized by the People's Council revealed that 200,000 Viennese approved this plan to legalize, in addition to the authorized market: a gray market where producers could sell their products after delivering the required quotas.

No one has money, no one can buy what they want or sell what they can, but the State—meaning government statistics—guarantees us that it is doing well. Indeed, the taxpayer cannot sing. He would be happy to see him at the end of reforms, but these reforms only begin.

A tax for reconstruction, thanks to which devastated cities will be rebuilt by 1949, will levy 200 million on rents in 1949 and 300 million in 1950, and so on. The taxpayer therefore sees once again the cost of living increase and the owner's meager profits decrease. If we count that 1,200 Viennese families are homeless,
3,000 households threatened with losing their homes, and that 413 families live in ruins, it is impossible not to contest the urgent need for this new tax. But will everything
not lead to further proletarianization and pauperism? Moreover, houses rebuilt thanks to public money will belong to the community—that is, to the State. Those who lost their property during the war will not recover; it is to the State since the taxpayers pay. That is logical.

A second tax, on the other hand, proves that the State knows how to change roles: a special levy to cover occupation costs,
a levy that has not yet been published in detail, which will fall to the community—which this time consists of the majority of taxpayers—the burden of paying for occupants' expenses. In unfavorable situations, the State no longer identifies itself with the community!

Finally, before taking his vacations, the National Council decided to create a wealth and income tax. The first tax will collect 1.5% on fortunes up to 50,000 sh; the same rate will be maintained for fortunes from 50,000 to 100,000 sh: during 17 years for fortunes between 100,000 and 600,000 sh; and for twenty-two years for fortunes above 600,000 sh.

The tax on income growth,
calculated for the period of 1940 to 1948,
will levy 5% on profits up to 2,000 sh; 0% until 5,000 sh; and 20% on profits over 500,000 sh. And so on, up to 50%
on profits above one million and a half. We estimate withdrawing 1.9 billion sh from a popular fortune of 10
milliards: they will be used to settle debts blocked since the war.

In other words, the State—because banks are nationalized—pays its debts with the money of the "community," which is once again private property. These who have increased their wealth from their fortune—7—are not all merchants—will pay their prudent caution, that is to say, work, whereas those who left their savings in the bank will reap the fruit of others' labor.
It is revolting in everything this involves. Far from denying the necessity of reforms. A country that has lost the war and
yes has never counted on affluent nations must gladly accept heavy sacrifices to rebuild its home. But this
home belongs to everyone, those who pay for it and want to live there—not just to the architects who build a facade barely staying upright. As for apartments,
they mock them.

There are no speculators, no "capitalists," nor careless legislators: one cannot doubt their honesty and goodwill as well. They
simply took too long to consider that the State is an end in itself. The people, you know how the people are, since phenomena described
can be seen throughout Europe,
should learn from those who are at their head that it is time to take a step back. But
I wonder if they are capable of this revolution in law. Because to do it, it is necessary more than just an empty wallet—it requires a taste for individual liberty.

Gustave Herrmann.

Accidents

A Geneva climber was struck by a rock block and suffered a fractured skull.
Geneva, August 27.

On Sunday, four Geneva climbers from the Alpine Club were on Mount Blanc when,
around 5:00 PM, on the path leading from Grand-Mulet Glacier to Aiguille du Midi,
one of them, Aimé Scheller, 36, a porter, was suddenly struck by a block that detached and
injured his head severely.
His companions remained with him at the injured person's side while the other went to seek help. An immediate column
brought the injured back to the station. Mr. Scheller received treatment from a French doctor and was taken down
to Bossons by car. From there, he was transported to the Cantonal Hospital in Geneva,
where he died on Monday morning due to a skull fracture. He leaves behind a woman and a young girl.
A dog cart against a motorcycle

* A small dog-drawn cart attached to a motorcycle, owned by Mr. François Savoy,
residing at Bossonens (Èribourg), crashed in front of a motorcycle mounted by
Mr. Max Veraud, pastor in Mézières (Vaud), carrying his brother inside. The motorcycle was overturned with its two occupants; the
gas tank caught fire upon contact with the acetylene lamp and ignited the clothing of Mr. Vernaud. An application
of soaked bags extinguished it. Mr. Vernaud had slightly burned his eyebrows and hair and suffered bruises. The
motorcycle, heavily damaged, had to be taken to the garage.
Severe automobile accident

Sarn, August 28.

A Zurich-based automobile occupied by four people crashed near Lungern. Its occupants were thrown out of the car, Mrs. Jenny-tHirlimann, 35,
a woman from a Zurich entrepreneur, was crushed in her chest. A doctor who happened to be passing by at that time
brought the unfortunate person to Lungern where she died on Monday morning.
One of the occupants was also injured.
An automobile smashed

* An Alpine Club car overturned Sunday morning near Sainte-Croix SUT Vuitobœuf, at the first major bend of the road below Château (Saimte-tCroix),
occupied by a small three-seater truck with two occupants and heading towards Sainte-Croix. It was launched
violently against the wall bordering the road. The occupants of the car injured themselves with superficial wounds; they
returned to Sainte-Croix but their heavily damaged vehicle had to be towed to the large garage at Remparts in Yverdon.

Almost three hundred meters away from home, this man noticed that he was missing his cheese grater; he returned. Upon his arrival, his wife appeared before him, soaked with milk, where Saugé entered and found Renault chained under the staircase. LA VIE DES SOCIÉTÉS CHEMIN DE FER SOLEURE-ZOLLIKOFEN-BEBNE.— An extraordinary general assembly of shareholders of the Soleure-Zollikofen-Berne railway company convened yesterday. It decided to reduce the base capital by 40%, from 3,862,500 francs to 2,317,500 francs. It also decided on the issuance of new priority shares worth 2,557,500 francs and a modification of the company's statutes. The reduction in capital aims to cover losses and create reserves. By issuing priority shares, it complies with the decision of the general assembly made on November 6, 1961, regarding which the Second Chamber of Civil Affairs of the Federal Court will still have to decide on December 12.

METALLURGICAL INSTITUTIONS S.-LOU— It will be proposed at an extraordinary general assembly convened for November 15 next, that shareholders increase capital shares from 6 to 9 million francs by issuing 10,000 new shares at a price of 300 francs each. These shares will be offered to shareholders at a share issuance price of 500 francs (Agence). NO PUBLIC DEBT IN SWITZERLAND FROM THE SOUTHERN EUROPEAN PIPELINE SOCIETY.— Contrary to some information, there is no question of an outstanding debt of at least 75 million francs in favor of the Southern European Pipeline Society in Switzerland. The negotiations that had been underway for a long time could not yield an agreement (Agence). Diethelm & Co, Zurich, participates in a subsidiary of Alcan. The Zurich-based company Diethelm & Co Ltd announces that it will take a minority stake in the Malayan Aluminium Company Ltd., the new transformation subsidiary of the Canadian company operating in Malaysia. Diethelm & Co Ltd, which has been active in Malaysia for about a hundred years, is the sales agent of Alcan Limited in Malaysia since 1947. As a commercial and manufacturing company, it has developed the use of aluminum in the rubber industry and owns an aluminum product plant in Singapore.

WESTINGHOUSE ELECTRIC (OVERSEAS) S.A., Zurich.— A new company was recently incorporated under this trading name; it will take care of the production and trade of electrical products, as well as technical research, distribution, and employment of any kind of energy. (Agence.) TED BATES & COMPANY S.A., Fribourg.— It has just been incorporated under this trading name a company whose purpose is to participate in all financial, commercial, and industrial enterprises, particularly advertising companies, and the exercise of any activity entering into the framework of an advertising house. The initial capital was set at 3 million francs. (Agence.) THE SWISS DELEGATION TO THE CONSULTATIVE COMMITTEE OF THE AEL.— The Swiss delegation to Vienna consists of Mr. Homberger, (vorort). R. Juri (Swiss Farmers' Union), Mr. Jucker (Swiss Trade Union), Mr. Meyer-Boller (USAM) and Weber, National Councillor.

Lausanne, Simplon. — The insurance for tunnel workers against accidents was concluded with Winterthur. Work continues under the best safety conditions for workers; until now, accidents are few.

University. — The first lesson from Professor Spiro's public course on the prophet Nahum will take place on Wednesday, November 2nd, at 3:00 PM, J I, Belles-Lettres.

Society of Belles-Lettres has just composed its committee for the winter master teacher 1898-1899 as follows: Mr. B. Vali, president of theology; Mr. H. C. Se, vice-president; and Mr. G. Gottschalk, secretary.

School Vinet. — We have a lovely pamphlet on the historical notice that Professor H. Vuilleumier composed about the Higher School for Young Girls, founded in 1839 in Lausanne, and which he read at the inauguration session of the new building of School Vinet on July 8th last year.

Outside the special interest this retrospective glance has for workers and students—old and new of the school—it presents a chronological review of the developments of the organization and programs of the first higher education institution for young girls in the canton of Vaud—and even all of Roman Switzerland, if we are not mistaken.

The cover is adorned with three lovely drawings by Miss C. Germond, depicting the three buildings that successively housed the school: the Madeleine, dominated by the cathedral; Bel-Air; and the new building on Rue du Midi. A few notes at the bottom of these vignettes recall the fresh cantata—historically, it too—sung under the direction of its composer, Mr. Justin Bischoff, at this inauguration ceremony.

Missions. — Miss Julie Deriaz, in Lausanne, has been appointed for five years as mistress at the central school for young girls in Tananarive, which depends on the London Missionary Society. She recently departed for Madagascar. Before her departure, she was responsible for teaching French to foreign girls at School Vinet.

Exodus. — A special train for the repatriation of Italian workers departs from Lucerne every evening at 9 p.m., from October 29th to December 24th.

Alpine Club. — The Diablerets section of the Swiss Alpine Club will hold a screening of light films with interludes of singing on Friday, November 4th, in the large theater hall. The color photographs give a great impression of truth to the views taken in the valleys of Bagnes, Anniviers, at the Dent du Midi, and Mont-Blanc. All friends of the club and of mountain sports are invited to this evening, which promises to be as instructive as pleasant and whose product will serve to maintain the cabins.

Construction. — Instead of a building demolished recently on the bottom of Rue du Pont, a construction almost completely made of iron rises. Except for the two side wings supporting neighboring houses, there is no trace of masonry. On the facade, powerful iron beams extend up to the roof, connected by other perpendicular beams forming an immense iron framework, which later will be adorned with windows and ice displays.

This construction is a product of our utilitarian century: everything has been combined to obtain as much solidity required, as much space as possible, and as much light as possible; nothing was sacrificed in aesthetics.

The architect is Mr. Verrey; the constructor, Mr. Zwahlen.

Literary Seasons. — The morning concerts that take place tomorrow in the concert hall of the Ca Santo-Theatre force Mr. Alphonse Scheler to hold his last two sessions on Tuesday. Therefore, tomorrow, Tuesday November 2nd, will take place the fourth session.

The program is very well composed. We find authors whose names have not yet appeared in previous editions: Alfred de Musset, Pailleron, Théophile Nicolet, Jean Valade, Ernest Depré, Charles Leroy, fables by Lafontainé, and even a fable by Napoleon I.

The race course.
Lausanne-Berne and return. All arrived in Berne on Saturday afternoon between 1:26 p.m. and 3:07 p.m., having covered the distance in an average of seven hours and forty-five minutes.

The pace was fast, a bit too fast, perhaps. Major Loys covered the distance in 6 hours and 25 minutes.

The temperature was favorable; dry and elastic roads. The riders, well-trained, put their feet down on strong ascents. Men and horses had well-deserved rest after ten hours of forced effort.

The first arrivals departed from Berne at 11 p.m. in their respective order. A light fog prevailed, but the moon illuminated the road with its soft light. No need to light the acetylene lantern, which some had taken.

Eight participants could not reach Lausanne due to their injuries—boating, bullet wound—and had to remain in hospital, who attended Morat, who stayed at Yverdon.

text: THE SWISS LAST COUNCIL OF STATES The Swiss married woman would retain her right of citizenship in Bern, 17 (ATS). - The Council of States council tasked with examining the new marital law, which completed its work on Tuesday in Bern, modified the draft proposed by the Federal Council on a few points. However, it accepted the government draft in its general lines and notably the replacement of the current property regime with that of participation in purchases. This matter will be handled by parliament in March. On the subject of names of spouses, the Commission joins the Federal Council in rejecting granting the option right, which would allow the betrothed to choose the wife's surname as their own name. Nevertheless, the woman will have the right not only to have her name followed (Favre-Blanc), but also to have it preceded by hers (Mrs. Blanc marries Favre). The Commission did not retain the option possibility due to the tradition that exists in our country. In federal Germany, where choice exists, only 4% of spouses use it. The new Swiss regulation will however facilitate eventual adoption by betrothed couples before marriage of the wife's surname as their own name. But good reasons will be needed for this (foreign consonant names, known names in commerce and politics, etc.). Regarding citizenship rights, the woman will receive, through marriage, the right of citizenship of her husband but without losing hers. A majority has formed within the Commission in favor of this solution.
